findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: Drop or qualify the assumption. The Context of the same design states that several business buyers share `orders@acme.example`, each with their own customer record and billing address; grouping on e-mail alone would fold those distinct buyers into one record and attach their orders to the wrong person. Choose a key that separates them (e.g. e-mail plus name/billing address, or guest-only records), or restrict the job to guest records, and add a spec scenario for the shared mailbox.
findings.title: The merge rests on "one e-mail = one person", which the design itself refutes

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The nightly job is a one-way door on customer data. Plan a way back before it runs unattended — a dry-run mode or report, a log of every merge (kept id, removed ids, moved order ids, removed field values), soft deletion or a backup — and a staged rollout, with a task and test for each.
findings.title: Records are deleted with no rollback, dry run or audit trail

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: Add scenarios for the cases that decide correctness — a shared business mailbox with different names and billing addresses, e-mails differing only by case or surrounding whitespace (the design lower-cases, the spec says nothing), records with equal `created_at`, and a checkout inserting a customer while the job runs — and state the expected outcome of each.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.evidence:
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: Only orders are moved; each `customers` row also holds `name` and `billing_address` (app/schema.sql:4-5), so keeping the oldest record discards the most recent billing details, and every order is then attached to an old address. Say which values survive (oldest, newest, kept as history) and how this personal data is handled; with the personal-data domain ticked and the privacy role disabled by `change.yaml`, no other reviewer checks this.
findings.title: What happens to the merged records' name and billing address is unspecified

findings.evidence: **Alternatives considered**: matching on name and address (fuzzy).
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: guest_checkout inserts a new customer on every order (app/checkout.py:7-11), so duplicates keep reappearing between runs. Consider, or explicitly reject with a reason, reusing an existing guest record at checkout; the only alternative listed also gives no reason for its rejection.
findings.title: The cause of the duplicates stays in place, and the simpler fix is not weighed

findings.evidence: - [ ] 1.1 Nightly merge job, verified by tests "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate"
findings.recommendation: Split the job (grouping, order move, deletion, scheduling) into tasks that each fit one session, and verify each edge case and the rollback path with its own test once the spec gains those scenarios.
findings.title: A single task with only the two happy-path tests
